Age-standardise survey percentages

Source: R/igm.R
stdprev.Rd

The percentage (or proportion, or rate) a group would have with the age structure of a standard population, from the estimate and published limits in each age group: for comparing First Nations, Metis and Inuit prevalences (suicidal thoughts, mood and anxiety disorders, heavy drinking) with each other and with an older population, for example, when the age pattern of the outcome is steep.

Usage

stdprev(
  est,
  lower,
  upper,
  std,
  grp = NULL,
  qual = NULL,
  conflvl = 0.95,
  scale = 100
)

Arguments

est, lower, upper

Numeric vectors (not column names): the estimate in each age group (and group) and its published limits.

std

The standard population, one count (or share) per age group.

grp

Optional labels, one per row: one result per group. Rows are matched to std by position, so order each group's rows by age in the order of std (sort by an age order, not alphabetically).

qual

Optional quality flags, one per row (a vector; see qltyrcd).

conflvl

Confidence level of the prevalence intervals (default 0.95).

scale

The upper bound of the scale: 100 for percentages (the default), 1 for proportions, Inf for rates.

Value

A data frame of class stdprev: group, estimate, lower, upper, se, usewithcau; attribute conflvl.

Details

With estimates \(p_i\), standard errors \(s_i = (u_i - l_i) / (2z)\) and standard weights \(w_i\) (the standard's shares), the standardised estimate is \(\sum w_i p_i\) with standard error \(\sqrt{\sum w_i^2 s_i^2}\), the age groups being disjoint domains of the survey (treated as independent: see indgap). The interval is normal, cut at 0 and at scale. A group with a suppressed or missing age group, or one whose published interval misses its own estimate, has no standardised value: the age group is not imputed. The standard should be the age structure of the population compared, or a common one: for First Nations, Metis and Inuit comparisons, the Indigenous population's own (cnsstd; Kumar and Tjepkema 2019).

References

Klein RJ, Schoenborn CA (2001). Age adjustment using the 2000 projected U.S. population. Healthy People 2010 Statistical Notes 20. National Center for Health Statistics.

Kumar MB, Tjepkema M (2019). Suicide among First Nations people, Metis and Inuit (2011-2016): findings from the 2011 Canadian Census Health and Environment Cohort (CanCHEC). National Household Survey: Aboriginal Peoples, Statistics Canada catalogue no. 99-011-X2019001.

See also

dastd for counts of events, cnsstd, indgap.

Examples

# made-up percentages in three age groups for two groups, standardised to a
# population of 500, 300 and 200 in those age groups
stdprev(
  est = c(12, 9, 6, 8, 6, 4),
  lower = c(9, 6, 3, 7, 5, 3),
  upper = c(15, 12, 9, 9, 7, 5),
  std = c(500, 300, 200),
  grp = rep(c("Nation A", "Everyone else"), each = 3)
)
#> Age-standardised prevalence
#> ---------------------------
#> Groups: 2
#> Method: direct standardisation to the standard population given
#> 
#>         group  estimate      interval      se
#>      Nation A       9.9  [8.05, 11.7]  0.9436
#> Everyone else       6.6  [5.98, 7.22]  0.3145
#> 
#> Highest prevalence: Nation A (9.9); lowest: Everyone else (6.6).
#> Their intervals do not overlap: the gap is more than sampling error.
#> 
#> Each group's prevalence as if it had the standard population's ages,
#> so the groups compare without their age structures.
#> Compare only rates standardised to the same population.
